podcast.title: Carpenters' "We've Only Just Begun" (1970)
podcast.body: The Carpenters' iconic version of "We've Only Just Begun" immediately became an "instant soft rock classic." Its enduring appeal allowed it to transcend its origins as a commercial jingle, solidifying its place within the genre's canon. "But the record was an instant soft rock classic that transcended its commercial origins."

podcast.title: Significant Radio Popularity (1975-1977)
podcast.body: Between 1975 and 1977, "over 150 radio stations in the United States had switched to soft rock or what some were calling mellow rock." This substantial shift underscores the genre's growing commercial appeal and the influence of corporate analysis of listener habits in radio programming during the 1970s. "According to a 1977 New York Daily News article over 150 radio stations in the United States had switched to soft rock or what some were calling mellow rock since 1975."

podcast.title: Post-1978 Rock Diversification
podcast.body: After 1978, soft rock became a recognized category within mainstream rock conversations, part of the extensive segmentation of music genres. "People were now talking about metal and Prague and folk rock, and soft rock, and country rock, and blues rock, and of course, punk."

podcast.title: Benefit for Dogs
podcast.body: Soft rock music is considered quite soothing for dogs, especially when reggae is not available. "soft rock is also quite soothing for them."

podcast.title: Defined as a "Mode" Rather Than a Genre
podcast.body: Kalefa Sanneh suggested that if soft rock is understood as "a tradition of songs often about romantic love, that are neither fast nor frenzied, and that convey a sense of intimacy," then it is "not really a genre at all. But a mode, important to a wide range of genres and fundamental to popular music." "If soft rock denotes a tradition of songs often about romantic love, that are neither fast nor frenzied, and that convey a sense of intimacy, then soft rock is not really a genre at all. But a mode, important to a wide range of genres and fundamental to popular music."

srcs.episode: Ep. 51 - The Softer Side of 70s Rock
Ep. 51 - The Softer Side of 70s Rock

podcast.title: Defining Characteristics and Evolution from Rock
podcast.body: Soft rock, also known as "mellow rock" or "safe rock," developed from 1960s and early 1970s rock music by adopting a "less aggressive sound," an "emphasis on the acoustic guitar rather than electric," and a distinct "emphasis on vocal harmonies." It expanded rock and roll by blending it with other genres such as country, R&B, and jazz. "That genre that we call rock music in the 60s and into the early 70s did take on a less aggressive sound. There also might be more of an emphasis on the acoustic guitar rather than electric, definitely an emphasis on vocal harmonies."

srcs.episode: Ep. 51 - The Softer Side of 70s Rock
Ep. 51 - The Softer Side of 70s Rock

podcast.title: Expansion, Not Just Restraint
podcast.body: Kalefa Sanneh, in his book *Major Labels*, posited that "the term soft rock could denote not merely restraint but also expansion as musicians mixed rock and roll not only with country as the Eagles did, but also with R&B and jazz." This view highlights the genre's role in broadening musical boundaries. "The term soft rock could denote not merely restraint but also expansion as musicians mixed rock and roll not only with country as the Eagles did, but also with R&B and jazz."

srcs.episode: Ep. 51 - The Softer Side of 70s Rock
Ep. 51 - The Softer Side of 70s Rock

podcast.title: Heart of the Night Transition
podcast.body: Poco's song "Heart of the Night" is identified as leaning "much more into soft rock," in contrast to their earlier "Crazy Love" which was pure country rock. "it was a bit different for their next hit heart of the night which means much more into soft rock."

srcs.episode: Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock
Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock

podcast.title: Olivia Newton-John's Early Niche
podcast.body: Olivia Newton-John was initially known as the "soft rock queen" in the early 1970s, a label she embraced despite it drawing ire from the country music establishment. "Now all grown up, I know that this was the era in which Olivia was the soft rock queen who pissed off the country music establishment."

podcast.title: One-Hit Wonders
podcast.body: One-hit wonders appeared across the Soft Rock genre in the 1970s. "We saw them in Glamrock, Disco, Soft Rock, Punk."

podcast.title: Origins in Pop and Folk
podcast.body: Soft rock is identified as being "born out of pop and folk," contrasting with hard rock, which emerged from the blues. "The soft rock is born out of pop and folk hard rock born out of the blues."

podcast.title: Radio Popularity
podcast.body: Soft rock songs with a laid-back groove were favored by radio stations in the mid-70s. "It's the exact type of soft rock song that radio stations loved to play in the mid-70s."
